acts.title: Text A · One sentence at a time
text: A team of conservationists based in Cambridge, who had been working in northern Myanmar since 2009 and who had almost given up on the project, announced in 2010 that they had identified a species of monkey which, although reported by local hunters for decades, had never been described scientifically.
That sentence is fifty-two words long, and it contains one main statement: the team announced a discovery. Everything else is attached.

The method for reading a sentence like that is mechanical rather than clever. Find the main verb — announced. Find its subject — a team. Everything between them is describing the team, and everything after the verb is what they announced.
Long sentences are not more difficult than short ones. They are simply longer, and they punish anybody who reads them in the order the words appear.

items.q: What is the main statement of the long sentence?
o: Local hunters had reported the monkey
The project had almost been given up

items.q: What method does the text recommend?
o: Find the main verb, then its subject, and treat the rest as attached

acts.title: Text B · Why journalism is written this way
text: A news sentence carries more than one job, which is why it grows.

The first clause has to say what happened. The subordinate clauses that follow have to say who says so, when it happened, and what qualification the writer wants on record — and all of it must be in the first sentence, because a reader who stops after one sentence should still have the story.

That constraint produces the shape you see everywhere: a short main clause, followed by a relative clause identifying the source, followed by a concession beginning although or while, which is where the writer puts whatever might otherwise get them into trouble.
Read the concession first, if you are short of time. It is usually where the real information is, and it is almost always the part that was argued about before publication.

items.s: A news sentence has to do more than one job at once.
The first sentence should still give the story if the reader stops there.
The concession usually begins with although or while.
The writer says the concession is the least important part.
The writer suggests reading the concession first when short of time.

acts.title: Strip it down to the main clause
text: A team of conservationists based in Cambridge, who had been working since 2009, announced a discovery.
Although the discovery of a new species is exciting, conservationists have warned that the monkeys were already endangered.
The supermarket, which had invited customers to blind-taste both kinds, claims the campaign was a success.
Two teenagers, who found the bag on a train, denied acting heroically.
While the physical health of the woman is poor, she is mentally aware and still tells stories.

items.q: Sentence 1: what is the main clause?
Sentence 2: what is the main clause?
o: Conservationists have warned that the monkeys were endangered

items.q: Sentence 3: what is the main clause?
o: The supermarket claims the campaign was a success

items.q: Sentence 5: which part is the concession?
o: While the physical health of the woman is poor

acts.title: Building adjectives, and reading long sentences
rule: Two skills, and they meet in the same place: a long sentence is mostly made of adjectives and adjective-like clauses hung on a short main statement. Being able to build the adjective and being able to strip it out are the same competence seen from two sides.
points: From verbs and nouns, meaning tending to do: impress → impressive, select → selective, object → objective.
From nouns: economy → economic, history → historical, medicine → medical. Note economic (of the economy) and economical (cheap to run).
Able to be: manage → manageable, rely → reliable. Negative with un- or ir-: unmanageable, irresponsible.
Opposite pairs: useful / useless, hopeful / hopeless. Not every adjective has both.
Find the main verb. Find its subject. Everything else is attached and can be stripped out on a first pass.
eg: -ical. Cheap to run. A different word.
The two directions of the same noun.
acts.careful: economic and economical are not the same word. An economic problem concerns the economy; an economical car uses little fuel. The same is true of historic (important in history) and historical (about the past).

write.q: Find a long sentence — from a news site, a contract, an official letter — and write about 180 words unpacking it. Quote it, identify the main clause, say what each attached part is doing, and then rewrite the whole thing in three short sentences. Use at least four adjectives built with the suffixes from this lesson.
plan: say what each attached part does
rewrite it in three short sentences
write.model:
The sentence I chose is from the terms of my mobile contract: “The Operator, which reserves the right to amend these terms at any time, shall not be liable for any interruption to service arising from circumstances beyond its reasonable control, although reasonable efforts will be made to restore service promptly.”

The main clause is four words long: the Operator shall not be liable. Everything else is attached.

“which reserves the right to amend these terms” is a relative clause, and it is doing something quite separate from the rest of the sentence — it is a second, unrelated power, hidden inside the first.

“arising from circumstances beyond its reasonable control” limits the liability, and “reasonable” is doing an enormous amount of work for one word.

The concession at the end is the only reassuring part, and it is unenforceable.

In three sentences: We are not responsible for outages we did not cause. We can change these terms whenever we like. We will try to fix things.
